messages.subject: [statnet_help] using nodemix in ergm-terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Avranil,

Good question.  Alas, there isn't currently a direct way of selecting a 
subset of pairings to model using nodemix.  There is a way to do it 
indirectly, however.  One can define a set of dummy attributes for each 
directed pair of actors (called an "edge attribute" in statnet) that 
represents whether or not they belong to a particular vertex-attribute 
combination, and then include this in the model with an "edgecov" term. 
This gives you the flexibilty to leave out terms representing any 
combinations you wish to ignore; it also allows you to combine multiple 
combinations within individual dummy variables to be modeled jointly if 
you so desire.  So it's a little bit of work, but very flexible.

Let me know if that wasn't clear and you need more guidance.
Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] new version of ergm on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hello statnet users.  I just got word that the source code for the new  
version of ergm, version 2.0-6, is now on the main CRAN server (http://cran.r-project.org/ 
) and it will propagate to the mirrors in the next couple days.  Also,  
the pre-compiled binaries will appear within the next day I think.

Thanks to several of you who have sent emails with bug reports in the  
past few weeks.  I believe these have been fixed now, but as always,  
please let us know if you find more!

In addition to fixing all the bugs, we have added a couple of things:
   -- The "asymmetric" and "mutual" model terms now take an optional  
categorical nodal covariate argument in case you want to count only  
those dyads that have matching values of this covariate.  This type of  
term may prove to be quite common for various network configurations.
   -- It should prove easier and easier to write change statistics  
from scratch, we hope.  The reasons for this are twofold:  First,  
there is a new protocol for writing InitErgm functions (i.e., the R  
functions that set up a term to be used in an ERGM):  These functions  
are now called InitErgmTerm functions and there are several  
illustrative examples as well as some comments in the file called R/ 
InitErgmTerm.R.  Note that the old way will still work, but using the  
new method will supplant the old automatically.  Second, there is now  
a growing list of C macros whose intended purpose is to make the  
writing (in C) of the d_xxx changestatistic functions easier.  The  
macros are found in src/edgetree.h and more and more of the functions  
in src/edgetree.c now use them.

Enjoy!
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenine.  As it turns out, we had noticed that this "contrast"  
argument was slightly awkward and it's now been changed.  Of course  
this doesn't answer the question of why you're getting the bizarre  
behavior you describe, but it should hopefully turn out to be  
irrelevant.

The new version of nodemix (which will be refected in the Morris et al  
paper when it eventually comes out officially in JSS) uses a "base"  
argument like several other terms.  Apologies to anyone who had come  
to rely on the "contrast" argument, since this will break any code  
using "contrast".  Here is the relevant excerpt from help(ergm.terms):

nodemix(attrname, base=NULL)
Nodal attribute mixing: The attrname argument is a character string  
giving the name of a categorical attribute in the network's vertex  
attribute list. By default, this term adds one network statistic to  
the model for each possible pairing of attribute values. The statistic  
equals the number of edges in the network in which the nodes have that  
pairing of values. In other words, this term produces one statistic  
for every entry in the mixing matrix for the attribute. The ordering  
of the attribute values is alphabetical (for nominal categories) or  
numerical (for ordered categories). The optional base argument is a  
vector of integers corresponding to the pairings that should not be  
included. If base contains only negative integers, then these integers  
correspond to the only pairings that should be included. By default  
(i.e., with base=NULL or base=0), all pairings are included.

This new version will be out on CRAN in probably a week or two, but  
you can download the beta version of ergm 2.0-7 that includes the new  
nodemix if you go to http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/code/

If you can't install R from source code, respond to the list with the  
type of operating system you're using and someone should be able to  
produce a pre-compiled binary for you.

I have to admit I haven't done a lot of testing on the new nodemix  
term, so if you find anything fishy please send another email.

Dave

Hi Jenine,

Here are my instructions for installing this version of the ergm package 
from the source, for Windows:

1.  Close R.

2.  Get the file (ergm_2.0-7beta.tar.gz) on the website that Dave mentions 
below. You can place it anywhere, although you may want it somewhere in 
C:\Program Files\R, perhaps in the lib directory for the latest version of 
R that you have on your machine.

3.  Gunzip it.  An easy-to-use free utility for this is win-gz 
(http://www.crispen.org/src/#wingz)

4.  Untar it. An easy-to-use free utility for this is 7-zip 
(http://www.7-zip.org/)

5.  You should now have a folder called ergm_2.0-7beta.  Note its 
location.

6.  Open a dos window (Start > Run and type "cmd")

7.  Navigate into the ergm_2.0-7beta folder.  (Basic dos commands: "cd .." 
to move up, "cd name_of_folder" to move down, "dir" to see what files and 
folders are avaiable in your current folder, "exit" to quit.)

8.  Make sure you are just inside the ergm_2.0-7beta folder by typing 
"dir"; the contents should be a single dot, a double dot, and "ergm".

9.  Type: "RCMD install ergm". Lots of installing should ensue.

10.  When it's done, you should be able to open R, and type 
"library(ergm)" and have the new version of ergm that you just installed 
loaded.

OK, I think that is everything.  Let me know if something doesn't work. 
It's possible that you will get an error at Step 9, which means you will 
need to tweak some of your R settings.

Cheers,
Steve

Hi Jenine,

A great question.  We really should make some tweaks to the print.gofoject 
function so that it only prints the lines up until everything equals 0. 
We don't need you to see 1,877 lines to know that none of the nodes in 
your simulations have degrees above 10 or so!

In the meanwhile, you can do it yourself by using the command:

gofobject$summary.nameofgofstat[linestoinclude,]

for any gof statistic of interest.  You can get the names of the gof stats 
by typing "print.gofobject" in R to look inside the print.gofobject 
function.

So for instance, if you just want to see the first 20 lines of the degree 
distrubtions, and your gof object is named model11gof, type:

model11gof$summary.deg[1:20,]

Cheers,
Steve

Dear Statnet developers and users,

We are trying to analyze an epidemiological network that is somewhat  
sparse and highly clustered.  Using a previous version of Statnet,  
we've obtained reasonably good fits with only 'edges' and 'triangle'  
terms in the model (validated via network simulation) that we sought  
to improve by implementing new user terms.

However, using the recent build of ergm and R, the same model now  
exhibits tremendous degeneracy.  Has anyone else experienced  
apparently 'worse' performance with the newer package?  We are  
secretly hoping that this is simply due to 'growing pains' in the  
current iteration of statnet, instead of being sent back to square one.

Best,
- Art.

Hi, Art -

Art Poon wrote:
> Dear Statnet developers and users,
> 
> We are trying to analyze an epidemiological network that is somewhat 
> sparse and highly clustered.  Using a previous version of Statnet, we've 
> obtained reasonably good fits with only 'edges' and 'triangle' terms in 
> the model (validated via network simulation) that we sought to improve 
> by implementing new user terms.
> 
> However, using the recent build of ergm and R, the same model now 
> exhibits tremendous degeneracy.  Has anyone else experienced apparently 
> 'worse' performance with the newer package?  We are secretly hoping that 
> this is simply due to 'growing pains' in the current iteration of 
> statnet, instead of being sent back to square one.
> 

The parameter space of the edge/triangle model has a very small 
non-degenerate region, so it is plausible that your issues stem from 
being close to the boundary of a phase transition (where tiny deviations 
due to numerical or other factors can produce substantial differences in 
behavior).  I would strongly recommend simulating draws from the model 
for a gridded region in the vicinity of your estimate(s), and examining 
the qualitative behavior of the system -- for instance, by plotting the 
mean edge and triangle statistics -- across the region of interest. 
(Mark has some nice plots of this kind in his degeneracy papers, and the 
approach is sadly underutilized.)  If your data falls near a region of 
degeneracy, then you should consider the possibility that the model is 
too unstable to be socially realistic -- unless, of course, you are 
willing to posit a sort of "fine tuning" hypothesis for your social 
system.  (There are probably circumstances in which such a hypothesis 
would be appropriate, but I doubt this is one of them.)

As a side note, I would also suggest checking (if you haven't already) 
to be sure that your MCMC is mixing properly, and that it has burned in 
adequately.  Mixing can slow down drastically when one approaches a 
region of "frozen" behavior, and initially salubrious results are 
sometimes found to be the result of insufficient burn-in.  By analogy, 
think of putting hot water in a freezer at 0 degrees Celsius: if you 
check on it after only a few minutes, you will find it to be quite 
liquid; a few hours later, however, it is frozen solid.  A very naive 
observer making only the former observation (and lacking the means to 
inspect the water temperature directly) might erroneously conclude that 
water does not freeze at 0 degrees Celsius -- the error, of course, 
would result from the fact that the system was initially far from 
equilibrium, and was observed before equilibrium was reached.  In the 
ERG case, the "hot water" corresponds to the initial network state, 
which may in fact be very "hot" relative to the MLE for the proposed 
model.  (Since the ERG parameters are essentially inverse temperatures, 
the analogy is quite close.)  As the MCMC evolves, the initially "hot" 
state may then "cool," in extreme cases locking into a very narrow range 
of configurations (which we experience as "degeneracy").  A degenerate 
model is "frozen" in equilibrium, but this equilibrium still takes time 
to reach; if we observe the state of the system before the MCMC has 
burned in, we may find that the system still exhibits quite a lot of 
non-degenerate behavior, and may thus erroneously conclude that the 
model is not actually degenerate.  As with our thought experiment, 
drawing the right conclusion depends on first allowing the system to 
equilibrate.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Hi Jenine.  Sorry about the insane version of print.gofobject that was  
in ergm.  I don't know if this addresses your question completely, but  
try copy-and-pasting the code below after loading statnet.  This will  
create a new version of print.gofobject and summary.gofobject (these  
will be in ergm 2.0-7, which should be on CRAN in a few days, after  
which time it won't be necessary to copy and paste!).  This version  
prints only the rows in which the stats aren't all zero.

Dave

##COPY AND PASTE STARTING HERE:
print.gofobject <- function(x, ...){
   all.gof.vars <- ergm.rhs.formula(x$GOF)
   # match variables
   goftypes <- matrix( c(
       "model", "model statistics", "summary.model",
       "distance", "minimum geodesic distance", "summary.dist",
       "idegree", "in-degree", "summary.ideg",
       "odegree", "out-degree", "summary.odeg",
       "degree", "degree", "summary.deg",
       "espartners", "edgewise shared partner", "summary.espart",
       "dspartners", "dyadwise shared partner", "summary.dspart",
       "triadcensus", "triad census", "summary.triadcensus"),
                       byrow=TRUE, ncol=3)
   for(i in seq(along=all.gof.vars)){
     all.gof.vars[i] <- match.arg(all.gof.vars[i], goftypes[,1])
   }
   for(statname in all.gof.vars){
     r <- match(statname, goftypes[,1])  # find row in goftypes matrix
     cat("\nGoodness-of-fit for", goftypes[r, 2],"\n\n")
     m <- x[[goftypes[r, 3] ]] # get summary statistics
     zerorows <- m[,"obs"]==0 & m[,"min"]==0 & m[,"max"]==0
     print(m[!zerorows,])
   }
   invisible()
}

summary.gofobject <- function(object, ...) {
   print.gofobject(object, ...) # Nothing better for now
}

## THAT"S ALL TO COPY AND PASTE!
